title: DAUTAJ v. SWEDEN
summary: In the case of Dautaj v. Sweden, the applicants, members of the Roma community originally from Kosovo, brought a case against the Swedish state. The case concerned their vulnerability as Roma facing potential harm upon return to Kosovo, a context marked by ongoing challenges for Roma and other minorities. The applicants sought protection under several articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, including the right to life (Article 2), prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment (Article 3), and respect for private and family life (Article 8). The facts of the case involved the applicants’ asylum claims in Sweden, which were ultimately not pursued further by them. On May 10, 2011, the European Court of Human Rights decided to strike the case out of its list, concluding that the applicants no longer wished to pursue their application and that no exceptional human rights concerns required continued examination. No violations were formally found, and no remedies were awarded. This case highlights the complex and often precarious situation of Roma individuals seeking asylum in Europe, reflecting broader historical patterns of displacement and discrimination faced by Roma communities across the continent.
